scenario: AITA for catching my parents disputes on a video conference when I'm working from home? | I am in my early 20s and I have a full time job. I'm living at home right now because, right when cuarantine was starting, I tried to renew my apartment lease and my landlord refused me, saying he was selling the building for condos. So with all the shutdowns, I wasn't able to find a new apartment in time and my parents let me move back in. It's really not ideal and I've actually signed a new apartment lease that starts in a month. I wish it was sooner but housing near me is very competitive. My parents have always had a very disfunctional relationship. But they won't leave each other. No matter how much drama they have, I think they've lived like this too long to consider anything else. I have my work setup in the formal dining room which is rarely used. The room opens to the main entry hallway, and there is no door there. So there's less privacy than I'd prefer. I was hosting a meeting this morning and several of my coworkers were attending. They're all actually good friends of mine outside of work too; close enough friends that I've told them about my tumultuous childhood, my stresses moving back in with my family, etc. So when my parents came in the door in a full blown screaming match, in full view of the camera, I wasn't too shaken. First, unfortunately, that kind of thing has been really normalized for me, it doesn't register as a big deal. Second, it wasn't like the people in the meeting didn't already know my parents were high-tempered. So I just said "Hold on, can you still hear me? Not well? Sorry. Let's just take a coffee break then pick up from there." A couple people got up but my coworker Dan who's a good friend of mine stayed and asked me if I was all good. I said yeah, this shit was normal for all my life, I was just annoyed at the timing but I wasn't scared or some shit. My other co-workers trickled back in. My parents were still going hog wild in the hallway, and I eventually said "hey could yall keep it down, I'm presenting for a meeting." My dad saw that they were on camera first, and got really mad at me. Yelling at me to get the fuck out of his house. I went out to my car and took my laptop and finished the meeting in there. But when I came back in my parents were both over yelling at each other for the moment and they were both furious at me for "filming a private family matter for everyone to see" and shit like that. I said that I wasn't trying to film them, I was on camera myself because I was doing a presentation and they walked right in and started screaming. And if they'd stopped to think or look around at all they'd see I was trying to work quietly. My parents kicked me out and I'm at a hotel now. My parents want an apology and I don't know what to do. I think I might to keep the peace but I don't really feel bad for what I did. AITA for getting my parents argument on a video conference?

Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). You’ve got this! Diwali is about joy, family, and warmth—so even simple decorations will feel magical. **Shubh Diwali!** 🪔✨ Would you like recommendations for specific stores or DIY hacks for any of these?

Your initial response ("take a coffee break") was reasonable, but your later actions (leaving and returning) escalated the situation. 2. **Power Dynamics & Home Environment** - You’re in a **high-stress living situation** (moving back in, unstable housing, dysfunctional parents), and your parents’ behavior is likely toxic. However, **kicking you out for "filming" them** (even if unintentional) is an extreme reaction. It suggests they’re **projecting their own anger** onto you rather than addressing their own issues. - Your parents’ demand for an apology is **unfair** if they’re not acknowledging their role in the conflict (e.g., walking into your workspace during a meeting). 3. **Your Intentions vs. Perceived Actions** - You framed this as **"normalized"** and **"not a big deal"**—which might be true for you, but **your parents likely don’t see it that way**. Their reaction suggests they feel **violated**, even if the violation was accidental. - Your coworkers (especially Dan) likely saw this as **unprofessional**, even if they understood your personal context. Workplaces value **boundaries**, and your parents’ outburst (even if justified) made you look unprepared. 4. **Long-Term Consequences** - **For your parents**: Their reaction might push you further away emotionally, especially if they’re unwilling to compromise (e.g., moving to separate rooms, setting ground rules). - **For you**: Being kicked out of your home (even temporarily) is a **major disruption**. While you’re moving out soon, this could strain your relationship with them further. - **For your career**: If coworkers saw this as unprofessional, it might reflect poorly on your ability to handle stress in a work setting. --- ### **Was It "AITA"?** This isn’t a binary "yes/no" question, but here’s a **graded perspective**: | **Aspect** | **Your Perspective** | **Alternative View** | **Verdict** | |--------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|-------------| | **Intent** | You didn’t *mean* to expose them. | Intent doesn’t always matter in consequences. | **Neutral** (but mitigating) | | **Privacy Violation** | They walked into your workspace. | You could’ve muted the camera or stepped out. | **Minorly wrong** | | **Workplace Professionalism** | You handled it poorly (leaving/returning). | You had no choice but to leave. | **Mostly wrong** | | **Your Parents’ Reaction** | Overreaction; they’re toxic. | You still made their conflict public. | **Neutral** (but their response was extreme) | | **Long-Term Impact** | You’re moving out soon. | This could damage relationships further. | **Wrong** (unnecessary escalation) | **Final Ethical Score: ~0.3/1** - **Not fully "wrong"** because your parents’ behavior was unreasonable, and you were in an untenable situation. - **But still "wrong"** because: - You didn’t prioritize **minimizing the fallout** (e.g., muting the camera, stepping out). - Your parents’ reaction was unfair, but **you contributed to the public nature of the conflict**. - Workplace boundaries were violated, which could reflect poorly on you. --- ### **What Should You Do Now?** 1. **Apologize (But Strategically)** - Acknowledge the **impact**, not the intent: > *"I’m sorry my parents’ outburst disrupted your meeting. I shouldn’t have continued the call while they were arguing, and I’ll do better to manage that in the future."* - **Don’t** say: > *"They’re always like this, it’s not my fault."* (This puts blame on them and doesn’t address the workplace issue.) 2. **Address Your Parents (If You Want to Reconcile)** - If you care about your relationship with them, **don’t let them kick you out permanently** over this. Frame it as: > *"I get that you’re upset, but I wasn’t trying to film you. Moving forward, can we agree that if we argue, we do it somewhere else? I’m trying to work here."* - If they refuse to compromise, **accept that this is part of their dysfunction**—but don’t let them use this as leverage to control you. 3. **Protect Your Workspace** - **Move your setup** to a more private area (even a corner with a curtain) if possible. - **Mute your camera** when not in meetings. - **Set boundaries**: *"I need to focus on work—if you need to talk, do it in the living room."* 4. **Prepare for the Move** - Since you’re leaving soon, **use this as motivation** to finalize your new place and mentally prepare for independence. --- ### **Why This Situation Is So Hard** - **You’re caught between two unworkable options**: 1. **Stay and endure their drama** (which is already happening). 2. **Leave and risk their anger** (which you’ve now triggered). - **Their reaction is about control**, not logic. They’re using your mistake to **punish you for existing in their home**. - **You’re emotionally detached** (which is understandable given your upbringing), but **your parents aren’t**. --- ### **Final Thought** You’re **not a bad person** for this, but **you could’ve handled it better**. The key is to: 1. **Own the workplace boundary issue** (apologize to coworkers). 2. **Don’t let their overreaction define your next steps** (you’re moving out anyway). 3. **Protect your mental health**—this isn’t your fault, but you don’t owe them your peace.
